q-214738.name: Question 1
q-214738.problem:
Solve the linear congruence $3x≡4\,(\text{mod}\,7)$ using trial and error. Express your answer as a nonnegative integer smaller than $7.$

$x≡$
{{field-1}}$\,(\text{mod}\,7)$
q-214738.worked_solution:
Since the modulus $n=7$ is fairly small, we can solve the congruence by trial and error. 

Substituting $x=0,1,2,3,4,5,6$ into the congruence, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}3\cdot 0 & ≡0≢4 &  & (\text{mod}\,7) &  & \times  \\ 3\cdot 1 & ≡3≢4 &  & (\text{mod}\,7) &  & \times  \\ 3\cdot 2 & ≡6≢4 &  & (\text{mod}\,7) &  & \times  \\ 3\cdot 3 & ≡9≡7+2≡2≢4 &  & (\text{mod}\,7) &  & \times  \\ 3\cdot 4 & ≡12≡7+5≡5≢4 &  & (\text{mod}\,7) &  & \times  \\ 3\cdot 5 & ≡15≡2\cdot 7+1≡1≢4 &  & (\text{mod}\,7) &  & \times  \\ 3\cdot 6 & ≡18≡2\cdot 7+4≡4 &  & (\text{mod}\,7) &  & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x≡6\,(\text{mod}\,7).$

**Note**: Any number congruent to $6$ modulo $7$ is a solution. For example, note that $13≡6,$ and this also satisfies our congruence:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x & ≡3\cdot 13\, &  & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡39\, &  & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡5\cdot 7+4\, &  & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡0+4\, &  & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡4\,\,✓\, &  & (\text{mod}\,7)\end{aligned}
$$

q-212057.problem:
Solve the modular equation $3x≡5\,(\text{mod}\,14),$ expressing your answer as a nonnegative integer smaller than $14.$

*Hint: You may wish to use trial and error to find the appropriate multiplicative inverse.*

q-212057.worked_solution:
Recall that a linear congruence $ax≡b\,(\text{mod}\,n)$ has a unique solution modulo $n$ if and only if $\text{gcd}(a,n)=1.$

In the given congruence, we have $a=3$ and $n=14$, and

$$
\text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(3,14)=1.
$$

So, our congruence does indeed have a unique solution.

To find the solution, we need to multiply both sides of the equation by the multiplicative inverse of $3\,(\text{mod}\,14).$ To find the inverse of $3\,(\text{mod}\,14)$, we compute the exponents of $3\,(\text{mod}\,14)$ until we get a result of $1\,(\text{mod}\,14):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{2} & ≡9 &  & (\text{mod}\,14) \\ {3}^{3} & ≡9\cdot 3≡27≡13 &  & (\text{mod}\,14) \\ {3}^{4} & ≡13\cdot 3≡39≡11 &  & (\text{mod}\,14) \\ {3}^{5} & ≡11\cdot 3≡33≡5 &  & (\text{mod}\,14) \\ {3}^{6} & ≡5\cdot 3≡15≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,14)\end{aligned}
$$

So, $5\cdot 3≡1\,(\text{mod}\,14),$ which means that $5$ is the multiplicative inverse of $3$ (modulo $14$).

Now, multiplying both sides of our congruence by $5,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x & ≡5 &  & (\text{mod}\,14) \\ 5\cdot 3x & ≡5\cdot 5 &  & (\text{mod}\,14) \\ (5\cdot 3)x & ≡25 &  & (\text{mod}\,14) \\ 1\cdot x & ≡1\cdot 14+11 &  & (\text{mod}\,14) \\ x & ≡11 &  & (\text{mod}\,14)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x≡11\,(\text{mod}\,14).$

$$

$$

Therefore, the solution is $x≡11\,(\text{mod}\,12).$

$$

So, our congruence does indeed have a unique solution.

To find the solution, we need to multiply both sides of the equation by the multiplicative inverse of $17\,(\text{mod}\,50).$ To find the inverse of $17\,(\text{mod}\,50)$, use the extended Euclidean algorithm.

First, we apply the forward reduction:  

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}50 & = & 17\cdot 2 & + & 16 \\  & ↙ &  & ↙ &  \\ 17 & = & 16\cdot 1 & + & 1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for the rightmost terms in the equations above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}16 & =50-17\cdot 2 \\ 1 & =17-16\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we back-substitute:

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =17-16 \\  & =17-(50-17\cdot 2) \\  & =17\cdot 3-50\end{aligned}
$$

We can write this result in modulo $50,$ as follows:  

$$
\begin{aligned}17\cdot 3-50 & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,50) \\ 17\cdot 3 & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,50)\end{aligned}
$$

So, $17\cdot 3≡1\,(\text{mod}\,50),$ which means that $3$ is the multiplicative inverse of $17$ (modulo $50$).

Now, multiplying both sides of our original congruence by $3,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}17x & ≡9 &  & (\text{mod}\,50) \\ 3\cdot 17x & ≡3\cdot 9 &  & (\text{mod}\,50) \\ (3\cdot 17)x & ≡27 &  & (\text{mod}\,50) \\ 1\cdot x & ≡27 &  & (\text{mod}\,50) \\ x & ≡27 &  & (\text{mod}\,50)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x≡27\,(\text{mod}\,50).$
